messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Suresh, a 52-year-old South Asian man and former maid, has been grappling with profound distress since an accident at work led to serious injury for one of his colleagues. The event remains etched in Suresh’s mind as disjointed snapshots, each a vivid picture that captures the horror and helplessness he experienced. One moment is particularly searing: the sound of metal scraping against concrete just before the impact that sent his coworker tumbling into an open elevator shaft. Each time these images resurface, they trigger intense feelings of rage within Suresh. The sudden and unexpected nature of these memories can be jarring, often leaving him shaken in the middle of his daily tasks. While working in a busy hotel kitchen, the clatter of pots and pans might instantly transport him back to that fateful day. He has come to dread such moments because they invariably lead to a deep sense of self-blame. Suresh's feelings of intense self-blame have left him questioning every aspect of his life’s meaning. The event happened because he acted in ways that, in retrospect, felt like an affront to who he truly is—a careful and conscientious person. This discrepancy has led to a pervasive sense of guilt and shame, eroding the value he once placed on his work and relationships. He had come to believe that nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore. His divorce further compounds these feelings, as Suresh’s wife left him shortly after the incident. She couldn’t bear to see him so consumed by self-reproach and unable to find any joy or purpose in their daily lives together. The weight of this loss has deepened his sense of isolation and despair. Suresh's negative appraisals are intricately tied to the intrusive memories he experiences. Each vivid flashback serves as a relentless reminder of his perceived failures, reinforcing his belief that he violated his own values and acted in ways antithetical to who he is. This loop has tightened over time, leaving him feeling increasingly trapped by these thoughts. What frightens Suresh most is the fear that this guilt will consume him entirely, preventing any chance at redemption or peace. His current state leaves him questioning if there’s a way back from this abyss of self-loathing and regret. The cumulative toll on his mental health and relationships has finally brought him to seek help, hoping for some respite from the unrelenting cycle of memory and self-blame that haunts him. Suresh is most hopeful for finding a way to reconcile his past actions with who he wants to be moving forward. He seeks support in understanding how to regain meaning and purpose in his life, and ultimately find a path towards healing.
